books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the account of Lowell mill workers in the course books. The facts are as stated in the books; the wording is original.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase: In the mill town of Lowell, Massachusetts, young women from farm families worked in textile mills, tending power looms for long hours in exchange for wages. Mill owners housed them in company boardinghouses and set rules for their conduct. Many of the women used their wages to help their families and to save for the future.

stem: Northern supporters of the free-labor ideal most directly feared slavery’s expansion because enslaved labor

options.text: would compete with free workers for land and wages.
would raise the wages of Northern factory workers.
options.misconception: Enslaved labor undercuts wages, it does not raise them; free workers feared cheaper competition, not higher pay.

options.text: would end immigration to the United States.
options.misconception: Background from the books: immigration surged in the 1850s even as the slavery debate raged; slavery’s spread threatened workers, not the arrival of ships.

options.text: would force the South to industrialize.
options.misconception: Background from the books: the South stayed agricultural on slavery’s strength; the fear was for Northern workers, not for Southern factories.

rationales.A: Background from the books: where slavery spread, free workers faced rivals who could not bargain and masters who could undercut any wage — so free labor’s defenders fought expansion.

rationales.D: Background from the books: the South stayed agricultural on slavery’s strength; the fear was for Northern workers, not for Southern factories.
rationales.general:
1. Recall the ideal: a free worker earns wages, saves, and rises.
2. Background from the books: free-soil men wanted Western land open to small farmers without competition from slave labor.
3. See the threat: slavery’s spread would plant that competition on the same land.
Remember: an ideal defends itself where it lives; free labor’s defenders fought on Western land.
